headline: Bond Rally Pulls Rates to a One-Month Low
tileReason: The daily 30-year average fell to 7.29%, its lowest this month, as Treasury yields slid on steady inflation data and a tech-stock selloff, and investors trimmed bets on a December Fed hike.
takeaway: Mortgage rates took a step down. The daily 30-year average fell 0.06% to 7.29% on Thursday, the lowest reading this month, and Freddie Mac's weekly survey dropped to 7.24% from 7.32%. The main driver was the bond market. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, fell from about 5.05% Wednesday to roughly 4.90%–4.98% at Thursday's close (sources differ on the exact level), its lowest in about seven weeks. September PCE inflation (the Fed's preferred gauge) matched forecasts at 3.6% over the past year, so there was no new inflation scare, and another round of disappointing tech earnings, this time from Amazon and Intel, sent investors toward the safety of bonds. That also cooled expectations for a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve (the Fed, the central bank): futures now put the odds at roughly 72% to 80%, down from about 83% to 88% right after Wednesday's meeting. This morning's Employment Cost Index, a measure of what employers pay in wages and benefits, rose 0.8% for the quarter, exactly as expected, with wage growth over the past year the slowest since early 2021. Working the other way, oil is climbing again after tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, with Brent crude near $115 to $118 a barrel. The 10-year yield is about 4.93%–4.95% this morning, little changed from Thursday's market close, which points to steady lender pricing today. Mortgage rates are still unusually far above Treasuries: the Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.17% above the 10-year on Oct 28, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. Over the next month the odds look close to balanced, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.afterLabel: Oct 29–30, after PCE, GDP and wage data
fedOdds.source: CME FedWatch via Trading Economics (Oct 30), KuCoin News/BlockBeats (Oct 29–30) and Get Leveraged (Oct 30); earlier readings via Daily Wrap and Admiral Markets (Oct 28)
fedOdds.note: Odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec 9 meeting jumped to about 83% to 88% right after Wednesday's hawkish hold, then eased as Treasury yields fell: about 80% late Thursday (KuCoin/BlockBeats, 79.6%), about 75% (Get Leveraged) and 72% (Trading Economics) Friday. Sources differ by several points, but a hike is still seen as the most likely outcome. The pre-meeting level was about 78% (Daily Wrap, KuCoin) or 73% (Admiral Markets).

drivers.title: Bonds rally as yields hit a seven-week low
drivers.text: The 10-year Treasury yield fell from about 5.05% Wednesday to roughly 4.90%–4.98% at Thursday's close, its lowest in about seven weeks. Mortgage rates follow longer-term bond yields closely because investors who buy mortgage bonds compare them with Treasuries. When yields fall, lenders can offer lower rates, which is why the daily 30-year average dropped 0.06% to a one-month low.

drivers.title: Tech selloff sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Following Alphabet's slide earlier in the week, Amazon's earnings disappointed and Intel's shares plunged on a weak forecast, renewing worries that huge AI spending won't pay off soon. The Nasdaq is down roughly 1.5% to 2% this morning. When stocks wobble, investors tend to move money into bonds, which pushes yields and mortgage rates down.

drivers.title: Inflation and wage data offer no new surprises
drivers.text: September PCE inflation matched forecasts at 3.6% for the year, with the core measure (no food or energy) at 3.1%. This morning's Employment Cost Index also came in as expected, up 0.8% for the quarter and 3.4% over the year, and wage growth alone is running at its slowest pace since 2021. Steady numbers, plus slowing pay gains, ease fears that inflation is getting worse, so investors trimmed bets on a December Fed hike to roughly 72% to 80%.

drivers.title: Oil climbs again on Strait of Hormuz tanker attacks
drivers.text: Brent crude is up about 2% to 2.5% this morning to roughly $115 to $118 a barrel after attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, with signs the U.S. may resume strikes on Iran; Qatari mediators are back in Tehran pushing for a deal. Higher oil feeds into gas and shipping costs, which raises inflation worries and tends to push rates up.

drivers.title: Strong economy keeps a December hike likely
drivers.text: Third-quarter growth came in at a 3.4% yearly pace, faster than the roughly 3.1% expected, and weekly jobless claims fell to 194,000, near historic lows. Two Fed officials voted for a hike on Wednesday. A sturdy economy with inflation well above the 2% goal keeps a December hike as the most likely outcome, which limits how far mortgage rates can fall.

outlook.basis: It's close to a coin flip, with a slight lean toward rates staying about where they are and no clear tilt up or down. In borrowers' favor: Treasury yields just fell to a seven-week low, tech stocks are shaky, wage growth is slowing, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.17% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%), leaving room to improve. Working against them: a December Fed hike is still seen as more likely than not, inflation is running well above target, growth is strong, and oil is climbing again on Gulf tensions. After a sharp drop in yields, some bounce-back is common. Big swing events: the November 3 midterm elections, the November 6 jobs report, the November 10 CPI report, and any escalation in the Strait of Hormuz.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average is about 7.29%, the lowest this month and down from roughly 7.5% in early October. A December Fed hike is still seen as likely, and the election, jobs and inflation reports in early November could bring bigger swings than usual, so it's worth asking your lender how locking, a float-down option, or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates eased a bit this week, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates slipped to a one-month low near 7.29% as bond yields fell; the election and the Nov 6 jobs report are the next big tests.
